A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the management of worms on farmlet C was more successful than on farmlets A or B, but that all farmlets were subject to occasional spikes in WEC and that the management of these spikes could be improved.
the use of a wide variety of anthelmintic products in combination with tactical WEC monitoring provided adequate control of gastrointestinal nematology in sheep on all three farmlet types.

the intensive rotational grazing (IRG) system (farmlet C), with the same management and stocking rate as the typical grazing system (farmlet B, but without the IRG), had lower WEC and required less anthelmintic use, but was not without problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of intensive rotational grazing (with a minimum of 2-weekly rotations), combined with regular monitoring of Wec, is the best approach to managing worm burdens in sheep.

the management of worms on grazing farms can be made more effective through the adoption of a combination of improved nutrition, intensive rotational grazing and strategic use of anthelmintic products.
grazing management is an important component of worm control and that rotational grazing can be an effective strategy to reduce the risk of worm problems in sheep.
